answer:
So I had this interesting conversation recently with a very senior IT leader at one of SaaStr Fund’s portfolio companies that sells into enterprises, especially larger ones (think $100m+ ACV).  They are doing well now, but when they started off, they didn’t really understand how to sell up.  To the CIO level, the VP level, the business process owners.
A few years back, we did a deep dive on “how to sell to CIOs” with the CIO of Workday,
a great session you can watch here:
But my experience is most founders aren’t sure how to do it.   They want their product to be used by everyone across an enterprise, ideally starting with the CEO and going all the way down through sales reps and engineers.  But most CEOs don’t know enough to buy software themselves, no matter how cool it is.  And most CIOs will want nothing to do with anyone who hasn’t worked in tech for decades, unless they’ve been truly vetted as part of their own network.  That leaves VPs of Sales and Engineering … often the #2 and #3 folks in any org.  Not exactly what many start-ups want to try to sell to.
The thing is, if you can get past them — they’ll almost always buy more than just your core app.  More features, more seats, more modules, etc.  So there is real revenue there, even with just an 8-person team.  It’s hard to close big deals without a brand behind you.  Or so it seems.
Here was our experience at Adobe Sign / EchoSign:
We closed some pretty big deals early on ourselves, but once we got past a few $500k-$1m deals, we needed a partner with us.  We added a local reseller, and then later, a channel manager, and then eventually, a global channel director.  Later still, we hired a Global Channel Head from Salesforce to build out a full channel strategy.

So I had a chance to interview several SaaS CEOs that have sold to CIOs recently (and one with $2B+ market cap) …
And they all said this:
“Don’t sell your startup to a CIO until you are ready for them”
What do they mean?
They mean there’s a social contract between vendors and customers when buying software, especially business process automation software and complex enterprise solutions. It means as long as both parties meet their end of the bargain … the deal will work out just fine.
The “Social Contract” in Sales
Here’s how it works:
Customer Side (CIO)
:
You want to buy something that can solve a problem or improve your processes. But what if that solution doesn’t work? You still need to make payroll, manage projects, run reports, etc. And you expect the vendor to help you through any bumps along the way.
Vendor Side (CEO):
You’re running a company, maybe even bootstrapping, trying to grow fast, hire great people, build something amazing. Your job is to deliver on-time and on-budget. Sometimes things break. That’s part of the risk.
The key point here is that when either side breaks their commitment, there are consequences. For example, if you miss delivery commitments too many times, a CIO might fire you. Or, if you don’t follow up after deploying a critical fix, he might never use your product again.
Can an 8-person Startup Really Deliver This Commitment?

Can an 8-Person Startup Sell to a CIO? Yes—If You Understand The Social Contract
When you’re running a small startup, especially one with fewer than 10 employees, selling into enterprises can seem daunting. Who do you even talk to? How do you get your foot in the door? And what’s the minimum size you need to be before anyone will take you seriously?
Well,
allow me to tell you a story that might surprise you:
The day I walked onto the Demo stage for my first demo event back in September 2010, there was no shortage of big-name CEOs on hand. But perhaps most notable was seeing three CIOs sitting front row center – at Demo Fall ‘09. These weren’t just any CIOs, either; they hailed from some serious enterprise giants: Workday, DISH Network, and Blue Drop Partners (BDP).
As I stood up there thinking this would never happen again, I realized something important: these enterprise buyers are often looking for new ideas and innovation. They’re willing to listen—and sometimes even partner with—the smallest startups if those companies demonstrate real value and expertise. So yes, an eight-person start-up absolutely CAN sell to a CIO—if you understand the social contract.
Here's how:

**Know Your Buyer**

Before trying to pitch yourself to a CIO, make sure you know exactly who they are and what their pain points are. Enterprise IT leaders like CIOs have very different needs and concerns compared to smaller businesses or individual consumers. They're typically focused on scalability, security, integration, and long-term ROI rather than flashy features or immediate returns. Understanding their priorities allows you to tailor your message and approach accordingly.

**Understand Their Constraints**

CIOs operate under significant constraints, including budget limitations, existing technology investments, compliance requirements, and the pressure to deliver tangible business outcomes quickly. Be prepared to address these challenges head-on and show how your solution addresses them without disrupting their operations or straining resources. Show them how you'll help solve problems within their existing infrastructure.

5 Interesting Learnings from Monday.com at $500M in ARR
Monday.com’s recent S-1 filing offers some fascinating insights into how they’ve built one of the most successful SaaS companies in history. As we dig through the filing, here are five key takeaways:

#1. They’re a Product-Led Growth Story Through and Through
We all know PLG is hot, but Monday’s results prove it works at scale too. The company started as an inside sales motion and today still relies heavily on that approach. In fact,
70% of their new customers were acquired by the sales team via outbound efforts
— showing you can scale this model without sacrificing efficiency. And just like any great PLG story, usage drives engagement which then drives upsells to larger accounts — driving retention and expansion.

#2. Enterprise Accounts Are Where It’s At
While everyone talks about SMBs being easier to sell to, Monday proves large enterprises drive the majority of value:
$50K+ deals represent ~20% of overall revenue
And even more surprisingly, these big deals also drive higher NRR.
But don’t get me wrong – small customers aren’t insignificant either.  While smaller customers (1-49 seats) grow quickly, they tend to churn faster.
So while it might seem counterintuitive, enterprise accounts become your secret sauce for scaling sustainably.

#3. Churn Is Actually Low Enough To Drive Cash Flow Magic
Yes, you read that right. Even though Monday doesn’t disclose actual churn rates, they do reveal something remarkable: despite relatively high turnover among “smaller” customers (
85% NRR for those), the average revenue per user increases significantly when moving to bigger teams.
The result? A healthy cash flow margin of 22%, making them one of the few public software companies generating real profits.

#4. Revenue Concentration Isn’t Always Bad News
Most investors fear concentration risk, but what if I told you it could be a strength?
As of March 31st, 2019, approximately 27% of their revenue came from three clients alone. Fast forward to Q1’23, and that number dropped to 13%. But here’s the kicker: even during that time, no single client accounted for more than 5% of their revenue. That’s diversification within diversification!

#5. Don’t Underestimate the Power of Organic Expansion
When you think about it, organic expansion isn’t much different from viral adoption. If users love your product, they’ll naturally bring in more people who need similar solutions. This happens organically because existing customers see value in using your tool for various projects across the organization. Monday’s data shows 35% customer growth over two years with only moderate marketing spend. That means customers find enough value to recommend it internally.

In conclusion, there’s plenty to learn from Monday.com’s journey. Remember that sometimes focusing on enterprise customers pays off, and having multiple monetization channels helps reduce reliance on individual segments. Most importantly, always keep an eye out for product-led growth opportunities where your customers help spread the word.

Can an 8-Person Startup Sell to a CIO?

We've all heard this myth:

"No one buys enterprise software without having a large sales force."

Or this variant:

"Only big companies with lots of resources can sell into the Enterprise."

I'd argue that's just plain wrong.

As I shared recently on stage at our SaaStr Annual conference, we have seen countless examples of tiny startups selling directly to very large enterprises – including some of the biggest ones out there.

In fact, when I look back on my time working with founders who went on to build huge companies, many of them started by going straight after those elusive, coveted "CIO deals".

Take a few examples:

- Workday sold its first major deal (which became a significant anchor customer) right off the bat – to their CEO’s old boss at Oracle!
- Dish Network took Zoom at $200K/seat (they are now worth over $100B+ today).
- BD&P (now part of Mastercard), was acquired for $700M+, they grew from zero customers in 2010 to thousands within three years.

One of these CIOs was actually at DEMO ‘13 where he saw one of these tiny start-ups pitch live!

Of course, there are challenges in getting past the security systems and IT gatekeepers protecting the fortress-like world of enterprise buying committees. But here’s what these stories show us: it IS possible for small teams to break through.

To do so requires something we call “The Social Contract”.

This contract is simply about understanding how your product needs to fit into the existing technology ecosystem inside any organization you're targeting.

Monday.com just hit an incredible milestone – crossing $550 million in Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR). But what's even more impressive than this number? The growth story behind it. At SaaStr, we love digging into the details to understand how companies achieve such massive scale. Let's take a closer look at five key insights that can help us learn from their journey:

**The Power of Focus on Enterprise**
At $550M ARR, Monday.com shows that focus on enterprise is paying off big time. Their largest customers now make up 72% of their revenue base. This concentration strategy allows them to build deep relationships, deliver customized solutions, and drive higher average revenue per user (ARPU).

What does this mean for founders looking to scale? It highlights the importance of identifying your target segment early on and focusing on building a strong presence within that space. By doing so, you'll be able to increase ARPU and reduce churn.

**Customer Concentration Works**
In contrast to many consumer-facing businesses where high NPS scores often correlate with low retention, Monday.com demonstrates that focused efforts can lead to incredibly high Net Retention Rates (NRR) across all segments. Even smaller customers show an impressive 85% NRR, while larger ones boast an astonishing 121%. What drives these results? Strong product-market fit, tailored support, and continuous improvement likely play a significant role here.

This reinforces the idea that customer segmentation isn't just about dividing customers by size; it's also about understanding their needs and delivering value accordingly. By offering specialized solutions, you can foster deeper connections with each group, ultimately leading to stronger loyalty.

**Efficiency Matters**

With 22% free cash flow margins, Monday.com showcases its ability to balance growth with financial discipline. In today's competitive landscape, efficient operations become increasingly crucial as companies scale. Maintaining profitability while investing in future growth requires careful planning and execution.

As a founder, keeping a close eye on operational efficiency will enable you to allocate resources wisely and maintain momentum throughout different stages of development. Remember, it's essential to strike the right balance between spending and saving – don't sacrifice long-term sustainability for short-term gains.

**Growth Through Diversification**

While most companies aim for one-size-fits-all approaches, Monday.com seems to have found success by catering to diverse customer needs. With 34% revenue growth, they're expanding beyond their core offerings without compromising existing markets. This balanced approach suggests that embracing multiple channels can help sustain steady expansion over time.

To adapt this strategy successfully, identify areas where your business can branch out without sacrificing core strengths. Be cautious not to dilute your brand by spreading yourself too thin, though – ensure new initiatives align with your overall vision and values.

**Key Takeaways**

From Monday.com's remarkable journey, several valuable lessons emerge:
* Focus on concentrated market segments offers greater opportunities for sustained growth.
* Prioritize customer relationships through tailored solutions and ongoing engagement.
* Maintain healthy cash flows by balancing investments with operational efficiency.
* Gradual diversification helps mitigate risk while fueling continued expansion.
* Understand your audience deeply to offer relevant solutions that enhance loyalty.

By applying these principles, you can chart a similar course toward successful scaling and sustainable growth. As Monday.com continues to break new ground, remember that consistent effort, strategic thinking, and an unwavering commitment to excellence are the keys to unlocking real success.
